definition:
The exaltation of Christ is the church's confession that the crucified Jesus, raised bodily from the dead, went up to the Father and now reigns at God's right hand as Lord of all. Protestant theology has traditionally spoken of two ‘states’ of Christ: his humiliation (his birth into lowliness, his suffering, death, and burial) and his exaltation, which begins with the resurrection and continues in the ascension, his session at the right hand (‘session’ is from the Latin sessio, ‘sitting’), and his return in glory. This study concerns the middle of that sequence, the ascension and the present reign; the resurrection and the return of Christ have their own studies, and the site's page on who Jesus is sets out the church's confession of his person. The Apostles' Creed says it in one line: he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty. From that place, the New Testament says, he pours out the Spirit, intercedes for his people, gives gifts to his church, and rules until every enemy has been put under his feet.

The biblical vocabulary is simple and spatial. The Hebrew yamin, ‘right hand’, is the hand of strength and favor: Moses sings that the LORD's right hand shattered the enemy at the sea (Exodus 15:6), and to sit at a king's right hand was to share his throne and act with his authority. Psalm 110:1, where the LORD tells David's lord, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet”, is quoted or echoed in the New Testament more often than any other Old Testament verse by most scholars' counts. The Greek words for the event are anabainō, ‘go up’ (John 20:17; Ephesians 4:8-10); analambanō, ‘take up’, used in the passive for Jesus being taken up (Acts 1:2, 11; 1 Timothy 3:16), with its noun analēmpsis in Luke 9:51; and epairō, ‘lift up’ (Acts 1:9). The words for his new status are hypsoō, ‘exalt’ or ‘lift high’ (Acts 2:33; 5:31), and the rare compound hyperypsoō, ‘exalt beyond measure’, found in the New Testament only at Philippians 2:9. The verb kathizō, ‘sit down’, carries the weight in Hebrews: a priest who sits has finished his work.
ot:
The Old Testament has no ascension of the Messiah in so many words, but it builds the categories the New Testament will use. Two men are taken up without dying. “Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away” (Genesis 5:24), and Elijah “went up into heaven in a whirlwind” (2 Kings 2:11), leaving his mantle and a double portion of his spirit to Elisha, who sees him go. That last detail matters for Luke, whose disciples watch Jesus taken up and then receive the Spirit he promised (Acts 1:8-11; 2:33). The pattern is thematic rather than predictive: the one who goes up leaves power behind for those who remain.

More important are the enthronement psalms. God himself is said to go up: “God has ascended amid shouts of joy, the LORD with the sound of the horn” (Psalm 47:5), probably reflecting a procession in which the ark, the throne of the invisible King, was carried up to Zion; Psalm 24 calls the ancient gates to lift their heads “that the King of Glory may enter” (Psalm 24:7). Psalm 68:18 celebrates the divine warrior who has “ascended on high” after victory, leading captives and receiving gifts. Paul reads that verse of Christ in Ephesians 4:8, with the wording ‘gave gifts to men’; the Aramaic Targum of the Psalms also reads ‘gave’, applying the verse to Moses going up Sinai and giving Israel the law, and though the Targum was written down well after Paul, many scholars think both reflect an older Jewish way of reading the verse.

The royal psalms supply the throne. In Psalm 2 the nations rage against the LORD and his anointed, and God answers, “I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain” (Psalm 2:6), declaring the king his son and promising him the nations as an inheritance. Psalm 110 goes further. David, the psalm's heading says, hears the LORD speak to one he calls “my Lord”: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (Psalm 110:1). The king rules from Zion in the midst of his enemies, and in verse 4 God swears an oath that he is also “a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek”. Jewish interpreters have read the psalm of David himself, of Abraham, or of the Messiah; the New Testament reads it as David speaking by the Spirit of a lord greater than himself. Psalm 8, which marvels that God has made frail humanity ruler over creation and placed “everything under his feet” (Psalm 8:6), is joined to Psalm 110 by the shared image of enemies and all things placed under the feet (1 Corinthians 15:25-27; Ephesians 1:20-22; Hebrews 2:8-9).

The prophets add two figures. Isaiah's servant, after suffering and death, “will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted” (Isaiah 52:13); the Septuagint's verbs there, hypsōthēsetai and doxasthēsetai, ‘will be lifted up’ and ‘will be glorified’, are the ones John's Gospel uses for the cross as the hour of Jesus' glory. And Daniel sees “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” who “approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence” (Daniel 7:13) to receive everlasting dominion. In Daniel the movement of the cloud-rider is toward God's throne, not toward the earth, which is why many interpreters hear the vision fulfilled first in the ascension, when a cloud takes Jesus from sight, and then in the return, when he comes with the clouds.
nt:
Jesus himself joined Psalm 110 and Daniel 7. Teaching in the temple, he asked how David could call the Messiah ‘Lord’ if the Messiah is David's son, quoting Psalm 110:1 (Matthew 22:41-46; Mark 12:35-37; Luke 20:41-44), and no one could answer. At his trial before the high priest he said, “you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62), and Luke's form of the saying makes it a present reality: “from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Luke 22:69). In John's Gospel the Son speaks of ascending “to where He was before” (John 6:62), and he tells Mary Magdalene on Easter morning, “I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God” (John 20:17). He tells the disciples it is for their good that he goes away, because otherwise the Advocate will not come (John 16:7), and John notes that the Spirit had not yet been given “because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

Luke alone narrates the ascension, twice. At the end of his Gospel Jesus leads the disciples out to Bethany, lifts his hands in blessing, and while blessing them is “carried up into heaven” (Luke 24:50-51); they worship him and return to Jerusalem with great joy. Codex Sinaiticus in its original hand and Codex Bezae lack the words about being carried up, but they are present in the earliest papyrus of Luke (P75) and in most witnesses, and most modern editions print them. At the start of Acts, Luke says Jesus appeared to the apostles “over a span of forty days” (Acts 1:3), and then “they watched as He was taken up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight” (Acts 1:9). The cloud recalls the glory cloud of Sinai and the tabernacle, and the two men in white promise that “This same Jesus” will come back “in the same way” (Acts 1:11). The longer ending of Mark, absent from the two oldest complete manuscripts of Mark, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, also says he “was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19).

The apostles' preaching makes the exaltation the reason for everything that follows. At Pentecost Peter argues that David did not go up to heaven, so Psalm 110 must speak of another: Jesus, “Exalted, then, to the right hand of God,” has received the promised Spirit and “has poured out what you now see and hear” (Acts 2:33), so that God has made him “both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). Peter tells the council that God exalted him “as Prince and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins” (Acts 5:31), says that heaven must receive him “until the time comes for the restoration of all things” (Acts 3:21), and Stephen, as he dies, sees “the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:56). Paul's letters assume the same confession. The one who died and was raised “is at the right hand of God” and “is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34). God seated him “far above all rule and authority, power and dominion” and made him “head over everything for the church” (Ephesians 1:20-22). The one who ascended “gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers” (Ephesians 4:11). Because God “exalted Him to the highest place”, every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9-10), and believers are told to seek the things above, “where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1). An early confession ends with Christ “taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). In 1 Corinthians 15:24-28 Paul adds the horizon: Christ “must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet”, the last enemy being death, and then he hands the kingdom over to the Father “so that God may be all in all”.

Hebrews builds its whole argument on the session. The Son, after making purification for sins, “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3); he is a high priest “who has passed through the heavens” (Hebrews 4:14), who entered “heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God” (Hebrews 9:24). Old covenant priests stood daily because their work was never done, but Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, “sat down at the right hand of God” and now waits for his enemies to be made his footstool (Hebrews 10:12-13). So he “always lives to intercede” for those who draw near through him (Hebrews 7:25). Hebrews 2:8-9 names the tension that runs through the whole New Testament: we do not yet see everything subject to him, “But we see Jesus” crowned with glory and honor. First Peter says he “has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him” (1 Peter 3:22), and 1 John 2:1 calls him the advocate, paraklētos, with the Father. Revelation shows the throne room itself: a Lamb “who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne” (Revelation 5:6), worshiped with the One who sits on it, and promising to share his throne with those who overcome, “just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne” (Revelation 3:21).

keyTexts.why: Elijah is taken up while Elisha watches, and his spirit rests on his successor. Luke's account of the ascension and Pentecost follows a similar pattern of departure and empowerment.
God installs his king on Zion, calls him his son, and promises him the nations. The New Testament hears it fulfilled in Jesus' resurrection and enthronement.
The divine warrior ascends on high after victory. Paul applies it to Christ, who ascended and gave gifts to the church (Ephesians 4:8).
David's lord is told to sit at the LORD's right hand until his enemies are made a footstool, and is sworn in as a priest forever. The New Testament's central text for Christ's reign and priesthood.
One like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. Jesus joins it to Psalm 110 at his trial.
Before the high priest, Jesus claims he will be seen seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds. The claim that led to the charge of blasphemy.
Jesus blesses the disciples at Bethany and is carried up into heaven. They respond with worship and great joy, not grief.
Jesus says his going away is for the disciples' good, because the Advocate will come only if he goes. The ascension is the condition of Pentecost.
The fullest account of the ascension: a cloud receives Jesus, and the angels promise he will return in the same way. The church's mission is set between the two.
Peter's Pentecost sermon: the exalted Jesus has received and poured out the Spirit, and Psalm 110 proves him Lord and Christ.
The Christ who died and was raised is at God's right hand interceding for us. The ground of Paul's confidence that nothing can condemn believers.
God seated Christ above every power in this age and the next and made him head over all things for the church.
Because he humbled himself to the cross, God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that every knee will bow.
Priests stand daily; Christ, having offered one sacrifice for all time, sat down. His session is the sign that his offering is complete.
The slain Lamb stands at the center of the throne and receives the worship given to God. The exalted Christ is still the crucified one.

history:
The ascension belonged to the church's rule of faith from the start. Irenaeus of Lyon, summarizing the faith the church received from the apostles (Against Heresies 1.10.1, around 180), included Christ's bodily ascension into heaven alongside his birth, suffering, and resurrection. The Old Roman Creed, the ancestor of the Apostles' Creed, confessed that he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. The Nicene Creed of 325 said that he ascended into the heavens and will come to judge the living and the dead; the form received at Constantinople in 381 added that he sits at the right hand of the Father and that his kingdom will have no end. That last clause answered Marcellus of Ancyra, who had read 1 Corinthians 15:24-28 to mean that the Son's reign, and even his distinct existence as Son, would come to an end when he handed the kingdom to the Father. By the end of the fourth century the Ascension was kept as its own feast on the fortieth day after Easter, as the Apostolic Constitutions prescribe, and Augustine counted it among the feasts celebrated throughout the church. Leo the Great, bishop of Rome, preached on the feast in the mid-fifth century that what had been visible in the Redeemer had passed into the church's sacraments, and that faith now follows him where sight cannot.

The fathers asked what the ascension means for human nature. Their common answer was that in Christ a human body and soul have been taken into the presence of God, so that the exaltation is the pledge of humanity's destiny, not only a reward for one man. The Chalcedonian confession (451) that Christ remains fully human after the resurrection made this a matter of doctrine: the one at the right hand is still the man Christ Jesus. Medieval theology treated the ascension as the completion of the work of redemption and the opening of heaven, and Thomas Aquinas devoted a question of the Summa Theologiae to it (III, question 57).

The Reformation turned the right hand into a point of controversy because of the Lord's Supper. Martin Luther argued that the right hand of God is not a place but God's almighty power, which is everywhere, so that Christ's body can be truly present in the bread wherever the Supper is celebrated; Huldrych Zwingli held that Christ's body, being a true body, is in heaven and not on the altar. The two could not agree at the Marburg Colloquy in 1529. John Calvin (Institutes 2.16.14-16, 1559) taught that Christ's body is in heaven and that the Spirit lifts believers to him in the Supper, and he gave the ascension and session a full treatment of their benefits. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Questions 46 to 51) names three benefits of the ascension: Christ is our advocate before the Father, our flesh is in heaven as a pledge that he will take us to himself, and he sends his Spirit as a counter-pledge; he sits at the right hand to show he is the head of his church, through whom the Father governs all things. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647, Question 28) lists the resurrection, ascension, sitting at the right hand, and coming to judge as the parts of Christ's exaltation, and the Larger Catechism treats the ascension, session, and intercession in Questions 53 to 55. Lutheran and Reformed theologians both developed the doctrine of the two states, differing mainly on whether Christ's descent into hell belongs to his humiliation or his exaltation.

Modern theology has pressed two questions. The first was cosmological: Rudolf Bultmann, in his essay New Testament and Mythology (1941), argued that the ascension belongs to a three-story picture of the universe that modern people cannot share and must be reinterpreted as a statement about existence. Many theologians who reject Bultmann's program also say that heaven is not a location within our universe but God's own sphere, so that the ascension is the risen Jesus entering that sphere, with the cloud as the sign of God's presence. The second question is ecclesial: Douglas Farrow's Ascension and Ecclesia (1999) argued that the church has often let the ascension shrink into an afterthought, and that taking Christ's bodily absence seriously reshapes how the church understands the Eucharist, its mission, and its hope. The Ascension is still a principal feast in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, and Lutheran calendars, kept on the Thursday forty days after Easter or, in some places, on the following Sunday.

differ.view: What is the right hand of God: a place, or God's power everywhere?
differ.body: Lutheran theology, following Luther and the Formula of Concord (1577), holds that the right hand of God is not a spatial location but the almighty power and majesty of God, which fills all things; Christ's human nature, exalted into that majesty, can be present wherever he has promised to be, above all in the Lord's Supper, where his body and blood are truly present. Reformed theology, following Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism, holds that Christ's human body, being a true body, is in heaven and not everywhere, while in his divinity he is present everywhere; in the Supper the Spirit unites believers to the ascended Christ. Both confess Chalcedon, both confess that the risen Christ remains human, and each fears that the other's view endangers the full truth of his humanity or his presence. The site's page on who Jesus is discusses the underlying question of how the two natures share their properties.

differ.view: Is Christ now reigning on David's throne?
differ.body: Most Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed, and Lutheran interpreters, and progressive dispensationalists such as Darrell Bock and Craig Blaising, read Acts 2:30-36 as Peter's claim that the promise of a son of David on David's throne (Psalm 132:11) is being fulfilled now: the exalted Jesus reigns as the Davidic Messiah from the Father's right hand, and his reign will be completed at his return. Classic dispensational interpreters, among them John Walvoord, distinguish Christ's present seat on the Father's throne (Revelation 3:21) from the throne of David, which they expect him to occupy in Jerusalem during a future thousand-year kingdom; they argue that the covenant with David promised an earthly throne among Israel and that it has not been set aside. Both read Acts carefully and both confess that Jesus is Lord now. The study on the kingdom of God sets out the wider positions.

differ.view: What does it mean that the Son hands the kingdom to the Father?
differ.body: In 1 Corinthians 15:24-28 Paul says that Christ must reign until all enemies are subdued and then hands the kingdom over to the Father, the Son himself being subject to the one who subjected all things to him. Many Reformed theologians distinguish Christ's mediatorial kingdom, the reign he received as the God-man to complete redemption, which will be handed over when its work is finished, from the eternal reign he shares with the Father and the Spirit as God, which never ends. Others, drawing on Revelation 11:15 and 22:3, where the throne is ‘of God and of the Lamb’, read Paul's handing over not as the end of Christ's reign but as its fulfillment, the Son presenting a completed kingdom to the Father and reigning with him forever in a new form. All orthodox readers affirm, with the creed of 381, that his kingdom will have no end, against Marcellus of Ancyra.

The traditional reading, held by most of the church through its history, takes Acts 1:9 as describing a visible bodily departure upward, the natural way for the risen Christ to show his friends that his appearances had ended and that he had gone to the Father. Many recent theologians who hold the same confession, N. T. Wright among them in Surprised by Hope (2008), stress that heaven is not a place far up in our space but God's dimension of reality, so that the upward motion and the cloud are the visible sign, suited to the disciples' eyes, of the risen Jesus passing into God's presence. Both views confess that the same Jesus, bodily raised, now lives with the Father and will return; they differ on how to picture the relation between heaven and our world.

errors:
The church has rejected several distortions. Some ancient teachers, including Gnostic groups the fathers opposed, held that only Christ's spirit returned to God and his body was left behind or dissolved; the church answered that the one who ascended is the same bodily risen Jesus whom the disciples touched (Luke 24:39; Acts 1:11), and that his humanity was not discarded but glorified. Marcellus of Ancyra's view that the Son's reign would end, rejected in the creed of 381, made the incarnation a temporary arrangement. Opposite to both is the tendency to treat the ascension as Jesus' retirement, as though he finished his work at the cross and now waits in heaven while the church carries on without him. The New Testament presents the ascended Christ as active: pouring out the Spirit, interceding, giving gifts, ruling the nations, and building his church.

Two modern distortions pull in opposite directions. One reduces the ascension to a picture of Jesus' spiritual significance, a myth about the meaning of his life with no risen body at the Father's side; the church's confession has always been that a real human being now lives in God's presence. The other treats Christ's present reign as a warrant for Christians to rule, as if his authority could be claimed for a party, a nation, or a cause. The New Testament's reigning Christ is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6), and his authority is exercised through the Spirit, the word, and the suffering witness of his people until his enemies are finally subdued, not through the church's grasp for power.
life:
The ascension means that the one who is in charge of history is the crucified and risen Jesus, with human hands that still bear the marks of the nails. Christians are told to set their minds on things above because their life is “hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3); that is not an instruction to ignore the world but a reminder of where their security lies when the world is shaken. The powers that seem strongest, political, economic, or spiritual, have already been placed beneath him, even though, as Hebrews admits, we do not yet see everything subject to him.

For prayer, the doctrine is a source of confidence. Believers pray to a Father at whose right hand sits a high priest who “always lives to intercede” for them (Hebrews 7:25) and who can sympathize with weakness because he has lived a human life. Because he has gone ahead as a man, the Christian hope is not escape from being human but sharing, soul and body, in the life he now has. And because he gave gifts to his church when he ascended, every believer has a part in the work he is doing through his body on earth, while the church waits, as the angels told the disciples, for the same Jesus to come back.
questions: Luke tells the disciples' response to the ascension as great joy (Luke 24:52). Why might they have rejoiced rather than grieved at Jesus' departure?
Hebrews contrasts priests who stand daily with Christ who sat down. What does his sitting say about his work, and what does his ongoing intercession say about the believer's relationship to God?
If Christ already reigns but we do not yet see everything subject to him (Hebrews 2:8-9), how should that shape the way Christians respond to injustice, suffering, and political power?
